title: Alicia Keys ‘and Friends,’ Victoria Monet, More Join Global Citizen Festival Lineup
description: Alicia Keys & friends, Victoria Monét, Yeonjun, and Yoshiki have joined the lineup for this year’s Global Citizen Festival, the organization announc
body:
Alicia Keys & friends, Victoria Monét, Yeonjun, and Yoshiki have joined the lineup for this year’s Global Citizen Festival, the organization announced on Thursday. 

	Taking place on September 26th in New York’s Central Park, they join previously announced performers Lauryn Hill & Wyclef Jean, Lenny Kravitz, John Legend, Lainey Wilson, Shaboozey and Tomorrow X Together. Additionally, Bill Nye, IZA, Jordan Fisher, Katie Couric, Lais Ribeiro, Marcus Samuelsson, Naomi Watanabe, Nomzamo Mbatha, PJ Sin Suela, and Vladimir Duthiers will make appearances, joining Rachel Brosnahan and Gayle King, and 2026 Global Citizen Festival host Hugh Jackman.
	

	According to the announcement, the festival is driving action to help solve three core issues perpetuating cycles of extreme poverty across the world: creating opportunities for 2 million children to go to school, supporting 1.5 million smallholder farmers, and providing electricity for 2.5 million homes. Tickets to the 2026 Global Citizen Festival are free and can be earned by taking action on the Global Citizen app.


	This year, New Yorkers can earn free tickets to the Global Citizen Festival by taking action and volunteering in our local community throughout September, including urban planting, beach clean ups, food donation and more. Partner organizations include Bowery Mission, Jamaica Bay-Rockaway Parks Conservancy, Pollinator Pathways, Support and Feed and 9.11 Day. To learn more and register, click here.  

	“There’s nothing like standing on that Global Citizen stage in the middle of Central Park, in my city, with people who love the world enough to show up for it. Every time we come together something shifts,” said Keys. “That’s exactly what the People’s Bill of Rights 250 is about. Passing the mic. Making sure every voice gets heard, and giving people the power to shape what comes next. I’m coming back with some incredible friends, and we’re bringing all that love and all that passion to the park.”
	

	“We’re thrilled to welcome this amazing lineup of artists from around the world who are generously donating their time to perform on the Global Citizen Festival stage,” said Katie Hill, Chief Music and Entertainment Officer, Global Citizen. “Some are joining us for the first time, others have supported our movement from the very beginning. What unites them is the belief that music has the power to move people to action, and they’ll take the stage in Central Park to help drive progress toward a world without extreme poverty.”

	Global Citizen Festival will stream live on the Amazon Music app, Amazon Music channels on Fire TV and Twitch, Prime Video, Apple Music, iHeartRadio, TikTok, Veeps and YouTube.

	The 2026 Global Citizen Festival is presented by Cisco. Major Partners are Authentic Brands Group, Bridgewater Associates, Delta Air Lines, MetLife, PayPal, and P&G; Production Partner Live Nation; Exclusive U.S. Audio Partner iHeartMedia; and Location Partner NYC Parks. Global Citizen Festival is produced by Emmy Award winning production companies Done+Dusted and Diversified Production Services.

	This year, global citizens have a new way to take action and secure tickets to the Global Citizen Festival. After completing their action journeys on the Global Citizen app and earning enough points, users can now choose between two ways to redeem them: enter the free ticket lottery, or make a $25 charitable donation to instantly secure their ticket. All donations will give back to New York City. Funds raised will go to City Parks Foundation to support their free programming and community engagement initiatives in parks across all five boroughs, as well as to organizations helping those experiencing homelessness across the city.

	Global Citizen is grateful for the support of media and marketing partners including Branded Cities, Captivate, GroceryTV, GSTV, Intersection Media, KEVANI, NYC Ferry, OUTFRONT, Seen Media and Trooh.

title: Cinema Guild Takes North American Rights on Ted Fendt’s ‘Foreign Travel’ Ahead of New York Film Festival Launch (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indie distributor Cinema Guild has acquired North American distribution rights for Berlin-based U.S. director and literary translator Ted Fendt’s “F
body:
Indie distributor Cinema Guild has acquired North American distribution rights for Berlin-based U.S. director and literary translator Ted Fendt’s “Foreign Travel” that will have its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival next month. 

	“Foreign Travel,” which launched from Berlin’s Forum section in February, is a portrait of a group of people linked together by friendship and a passion for the books of Italian writer Anna Maria Ortese. Shot over the course of a one-year period in Berlin and Potsdam, it revolves around a young woman named Leonia who, “after returning from a trip to Naples where she sought to forget her past,” dives deep into Ortese’s body of work, according to the synopsis. “She and her friends meet to discuss Ortese’s books ‘The Port of Toledo’ and ‘Iguana,’,” it adds, “revealing the fine line between a passion for literature as a way of engaging with the world and a way of sublimating one’s demons.” “At once hermetic and open, ascetic and sensuous, Fendt’s fourth feature is a beautiful evolution of the work he’s been making for over a decade,” said Cinema Guild’s Edward McCarry in a statement. “We’re delighted to help bring this film—and by extension all of Fendt’s films—to a larger audience.”

	Fendt’s previous films include “Short Stay” (2016), “Classical Period” (2018), and “Outside Noise” (2021).


	Cinema Guild is planning to release “Foreign Travel” theatrically on a new 16mm print in 2027.

	The deal was negotiated by Edward McCarry and Peter Kelly of Cinema Guild with Hans Broich of Superzoom Film.

	Cinema Guild’s upcoming releases include Hong Sangsoo’s “The Day She Returns” and “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes” and Éric Baudelaire’s “For the Moon.”

schema.headline: Cinema Guild Takes North American Rights on Ted Fendt’s ‘Foreign Travel’ Ahead of New York Film Festival Launch (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Sky’s Defense-News App Could Help Old-School Media Launch Offense Against Creators
description: Deborah Haynes covers serious stuff, like foreign affairs, national security and defense — the sorts of topics that might not make good fodder for a
body:
Deborah Haynes covers serious stuff, like foreign affairs, national security and defense — the sorts of topics that might not make good fodder for a snarky newsletter or a hot-talk podcast. Even so, her employer, Sky News, has some new ideas about how to reach viewers that could put Haynes in contact with viewers similar to the ones that enjoy those up-and-coming creator ventures.

	Sky News, part of Comcast, on Thursday launched a new mobile app all about defense and security, with Haynes and others at its center. Subscriptions to the new “Defence Insider” cost £14.99 per month — about $20.31 in U.S. dollars, more than the fees for a similar subscription to CNN, Fox Nation, or the recently introduced MS NOW “Membership.” Indeed, the price of getting “Defence Insider” is on par with the highest-cost monthly dues for HBO Max or Netflix.
	

	Sky News thinks subscribers will see the value. “We think that the quality and exclusivity of the content represents a really good value for consumers, says Andrew Thomson, executive director of business operations at Sky News, during a recent interview. The company thinks people eager to learn more about the app’s topics will crave an experience that puts high level analysis “right in the palm of their hands.”


	Other mainstream news outlets might pay attention to what Sky News is doing, particularly in a moment when many top journalists are launching independent publications, podcasts and communities — and keeping the money they earn for themselves. Subscribers to “Defence Insider” get video reporting; expert briefings and explainers; interviews with defense experts and decision makers; access to live events and subscriber-only experiences; and the opportunity to ask Sky News journalists and analysts questions directly via online features and community discussions.
	

	“A lot of people talk about direct-to-consumer,” says Jane Ferguson, founder and CEO of Noosphere, a creator media company that has worked to develop the technology Sky News is utilizing for its venture. For legacy media outlets, she says, Sky News’ ‘Defence Weekly” represents “the first true architecture for it.”

	Noosphere, which also operates a creator venture that bundles journalists including Chuck Todd and Brody Mullins under a single subscription, is in talks with “major legacy media in the U.S.,” she says about providing similar technology that would allow mainstream journalists to publish information and video more quicky than is the norm. Ferguson believes such technology would give reporters at traditional news organizations something they truly covet: the chance to work in more entrepreneurial fashion like their counterparts who lead podcasts and newsletters.

	“The big fear right now is a loss of talent to third-party platforms — podcasting, your Substacks, social media,” she says. “The truth is if you’re a journalist, it’s tempting to go out on your own, but what you really want is a little more freedom, but to remain with a respected brand.” The promotion and publicity that larger news organizations can bring to bear is just one consideration, as is an ability to put new content directly in front of a large audience that has already been cultivated.

	For Sky, the issue is less about trying to keep talent and more about showing up in relevant ways for news aficionados. “How can we help audiences go much deeper with us in a new environment?” asks Thomson, who notes such activity can help diversify revenue. “We know that consumers are increasingly turning to faces and voices they know, and they trust and they respect and they feel they can make a relationship with,” he says. While the goal isn’t necessarily retention of talent, he says, “if that was a byproduct, that is great.”

	Some mainstream news companies already seem open to new types of arrangements. NBC News earlier this year stuck an alliance with technology journalist Joanna Stern, who recently launched her own venture, “New Things.” Fox News Channel last year struck a deal that makes the team behind the popular conservative podcast “Ruthless” part of its array of contributors. MS NOW’s new “Membership” subscription product gives customers the chance to ask questions directly of Rachel Maddow, Stephanie Ruhle and others every day — on video.
	

	Some of the nation’s biggest news purveyors are scrambling to find ways to appeal to younger audiences who gravitate more readily to digital outlets that may only have months or a few years of traction. Magid, a longtime consultant that works with local TV news operations and large media companies, has urged news executives to take note of the growing faith viewers place in individual anchors, influencers and creators over news brands.

	Before launching its new “Membership,” MS NOW executives tapped 18,000 news consumers to find out what features would draw them to subscribe. Many of the interviewees were looking for more than just a place to find the daily news cycle, says Rebecca Kutler, president of MS NOW. “We saw there was a need out there for people who are fans of our content and are looking for more connection points in their life, outside of just what they’re getting on TV or online,” she says.

	Jen Psaki, the MS NOW 9 p.m. anchor, has been experimenting with a quick-hit program on YouTube. “I’m delighted to be in a ponytail with my glasses on, just talking 15 minutes about the issues of the day or the stories of the week or the things that haven’t been covered,” she says. “Will that work or not work? We’ll see, right?”  But Psaki says she is often approached by younger people who tell her, “I love what you do on YouTube. Like, what else are you doing now?”

	Media outlets like MS NOW and others have good reasons to keep expert journalists under their corporate umbrella. “If you have a walled garden of your own content, it means it’s much harder to scrape” by artificial intelligence, says Ferguson. “If your content is in a walled garden, that elevates your brand. You can guarantee to the public that it’s human-generated expertise.”

	At Sky, the work people like Haynes and military analyst Michael Clarke do will also be kept free (or as free as possible) from the vicissitudes of social media. In the company’s new subscription product, there is no flurry of random off-topic comments posted by unidentified users. Instead, subscribers pick the expert they wish to query, says Thomson, and ask them about the information they want. Analysts and journalists get to pick the question they want to answer, either via short video or in a text-based response, and none of it is posted publicly until a response is crafted and checked,
	

	Such technology brings with it the potential for new economic models to be created by legacy media. Ferguson can envision revenue-sharing arrangements for journalists whose reputation and expertise draws the types of crowds that help fuel media coffers.

	“Defence Insider” isn’t meant to vie with specialist publications like Jane’s Defence Weekly, says Thomson, but he expects the new product to appeal to “defense industry professionals, but also the public sector and policy audiences.”  Sky was encouraged by audience interest in “The Wargame,” a five-part podcast it co-produced that envisioned how a Russian attack on the U.K. might play out and tapped the expertise of former ministers and military chiefs among others. Haynes played a critical role in telling the story to listeners — just as she will have a central part in the new venture as well.

schema.headline: Sky’s Defense-News App Could Help Old-School Media Launch Offense Against Creators

title: Lee Pace on Romancing Sandra Bullock in ‘Practical Magic 2,’ Life as a Leading Man and His 6-Foot-Five Star Power: ‘I’m a Monster!’
description:

	“I’m lying on this bed, naked,” Pa
body:
The first scene Lee Pace shot in “Practical Magic 2” required plenty of prosthetic tattoos — and zero wardrobe.

	“I’m lying on this bed, naked,” Pace says with a laugh, “and the two of them come into the room and do some magic.” In the sequel to 1998’s beloved fantasy film, Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman return as two sisters who are witches. They travel to England to seek help from Pace’s professor of magic, who’s under the effects of a curse, immobilized.
	

	This immobilization presented an acting challenge for Pace as a fan of both stars. “I’m laying there with my eyes closed, hearing their voices — their beautiful, distinctive voices.” His voice drips with admiration. “And it was definitely a moment: Wow, this is going to happen.”


	Kidman’s and Bullock’s characters marvel at the naked 6-foot-5 Pace, and a rollicking comic set-piece begins, as they use their powers to bring him to life. Pace, who’d been cast over Zoom and arrived on set only days before, was suddenly thrashing about nude with two actresses he’d adored from afar — forcing himself to be in the moment despite it all. His eyes were meant to be closed, but, Pace says, “it was impossible not to peek a little bit.” 

	Pace is at once wildly prolific — especially lately — and surprisingly unjaded. When he’s discussing “Practical Magic 2,” he seems like a fan as much as an actor. It’s an almost distant memory though: He is meeting up with me in New York in mid-July on a dayslong break between shoots in Prague and New Zealand, having just wrapped Season 4 of Apple TV’s science fiction saga “Foundation,” in which he’s played a succession of powerful, interrelated characters. He’s about to start the next “Lord of the Rings” sequel, 2027’s Andy Serkis-directed “The Hunt for Gollum,” where he’s reprising his role as elf-king Thranduil. 
	



	

									Ryan Pfluger for Variety
	



	This relentless schedule makes clear that Pace, at 47, is on the brink of a new kind of stardom. He’s been a pathbreaker as a queer leading man. Since his Emmy-nominated breakthrough in the swoony cult hit “Pushing Daisies” from 2007 to 2009, he’s been a franchise-ready character actor, exploring heroism in “Lord of the Rings,” villainy in “Guardians of the Galaxy” and something in between as the complex antihero of AMC’s origin-of-computing drama “Halt and Catch Fire.” Along the way, he’s made pit stops on Broadway in revivals of “The Normal Heart” (2011) and “Angels in America” (2018). He’s been the thinking fan’s thirst trap. But with “Practical Magic 2,” Pace checks the final box — he can be funny too. 

	Part of the humor is that Pace, so physically daunting, is far less powerful than the sisters. Instead, he gets the chance to be grounded, wry and, once his Dr. Ian Wright wakes up and settles into the story, yearningly romantic opposite Bullock. Her character’s curse is that any man she loves will die, setting up a painfully high-stakes will-they-or-won’t-they. 

	Seated at one of his favorite restaurants in lower Manhattan, Pace is, unavoidably, massive. It’s the first thing one notices about him, even before his diaphanous, drapey garments — like what Jonathan Anderson might design for Tatooine Fashion Week. Pace demurs when asked about his height: He’s only ever been himself, after all, so he doesn’t feel tall. “I don’t even always know it,” he says, “but then I see a picture, and I’m like, I’m a monster!” These last words are delivered in a conspiratorial whisper; he has a surprisingly soft-spoken cadence that makes anyone in conversation lean in closer. Once they do, they tend to find broad-ranging references to film, theater, literature and philosophy from a mind not content to sit still. 

	“Something about his voice is sensual, disarming and frightening at the same time,” his friend Colman Domingo says. (They appeared together in last year’s “The Running Man,” in which Pace played a masked killer hunting Glen Powell’s protagonist.) “He’s devastatingly gorgeous, and when he speaks to you, it’s as if he’s speaking only to you. You always feel like he’s telling you a secret. He’s always a little naughty.” 
	

	Learning to work around his body was a challenge for Pace at first. His first major onscreen credit was in the 2003 Showtime film “Soldier’s Girl,” as Calpernia Addams, a real-life trans woman who falls in love with an Army private. Pace, early on, told director Frank Pierson, “I don’t know how I make my big body do this.” Pierson, according to Pace, said, “You need to believe you’re a woman. And really fall in love — believe you are.” 

	Pace practiced that once again on the Leavesden set of “Practical Magic 2,” outside London. “There’s technique involved, but it’s fun to fall in love,” Pace says. “It’s fun to see the best in someone and see them smile back. It’s pretty simple to me.” The sequel marked a bit of sunshine amid the dark universes in which Pace often romps. “I always think it’s funny when you hear actors say, ‘Oh, the kissing scenes are the worst.’” He grins. “I think they’re great.”


	Pace makes friends on set easily, in part because he wears his characters lightly. “I didn’t realize it was the same guy who was in the mask in the rehearsals, he had such menace in his body,” says Domingo. “Then meeting him, he’s so lithe, like a dancer — elegant and romantic.” 

	Some of Pace’s earliest friendships were rooted in acting too. At his high school in suburban Houston, he found himself in an intense theater program. “There was this culture among the students: reading the plays very seriously, reading Uta Hagen and Stanislavsky.” (I ask whether he’s read Susan Choi’s 2019 novel “Trust Exercise,” about tensions among high school theater students in Houston. He has, of course.) Pace and his classmates read reviews of Broadway shows they’d never see, like the 1993 staging of “Angels in America” and the 1995 revival of “The Heiress,” with its much-heralded Cherry Jones star turn. Now, Jones will appear on the forthcoming season of “Foundation,” due next year. “I laughed about the fact that I knew her as a legendary person before even seeing her work!” Pace says.



	

									Ryan Pfluger for Variety
	



	Jones says she’d never heard Pace’s story about Houston-area teens venerating her. But she wasn’t surprised. “Far, far from the lights of Broadway, it would be a thrilling thing,” the Tennessee-raised actress says. “If I had read a review about Colleen Dewhurst, I would have had the same reaction, I’m sure.” She shares an affinity with Pace as strivers stuck, early on, somewhere they felt they might not quite fit in: “We’re both from Southern states that start with the letter ‘T.’” 

	Jones and Pace are, more specifically, both queer artists who emerged from the Deep South. One night, after they first met, Jones asked Pace, “How did you deal with that, growing up in Texas?” She remembers him saying, “I didn’t give a fuck what anybody thought.” 
	

	“That’s the essence of the man,” she goes on. “He has a joy and a confidence. The greatest trailblazers of all are oblivious to any slings and arrows. Anything coming their way, they don’t even bother with them.” 

	Oblivious may be overstating the case slightly. Pace remains wounded by a media imbroglio that happened during his “Angels in America” run in 2018, when a profile writer for W Magazine asked him his sexual orientation. Pace acknowledged that he’d dated both men and women, but called the question “intrusive,” kicking off a debate over the concept of outing and whether Pace had been outed unfairly. 

	His time in the play was already intense: Playing Joe Pitt, an ambitious but closeted Mormon Republican, Pace felt so inside his character that the verbal blows he exchanged with castmates really landed. “There were scenes where it’s a fight happening, but you are fighting,” he says. “I’m proud of that work, even though it hurt to be called a liar. It was hard to walk in his shoes.” Joe, hiding his true self, was accurately called out. And Pace felt as if the media were suddenly making the same accusation about him. “Why do I have to make some kind of statement about myself?” he asks. “You don’t want to be called a liar, but I received advice early on that if you want to have longevity as an actor — play the characters, do the work.”

	Playwright Tony Kushner had long marveled at Pace’s ability to embody contradiction: In the casting process for 2012’s “Lincoln,” which Kushner wrote, Pace got the part of the charismatic, virulently pro-slavery congressman Fernando Wood. “Wouldn’t it be great if instead of having a villain, we had someone odd, delightful, charming and witty?” Kushner recalls thinking. As for the sphere of privacy around Pace that came under threat during “Angels,” Kushner says, “He’s an actor who has become famous and celebrated at a moment when what it means to be an actor and your relationship to the audience has been undergoing all sorts of changes. He’s handling all that very nicely.” 

	Pace has boundaries, but he’s hardly closed off to the world around him. One of the great pleasures of working on the “Lord of the Rings” movies, he says, is his bond with Ian McKellen, the 87-year-old screen legend who plays Gandalf — and an out gay actor who’s similarly hopped between high fantasy and a life onstage. It’s another pinch-me moment for the kid from suburban Houston, who once drove into the city to see McKellen’s 1995 film “Richard III.” “What was it like doing ‘Amadeus’?” Pace remembers asking him. “Tell me about Magneto. Tell me about producing ‘Richard III.’ To say it’s school is not enough. To say that it’s falling in love — it’s not enough.” 
	

	Acting can be difficult, but love is the easy part. I ask Pace about his relationship to clothing — like the baffling, dazzling outfit he’s wearing at lunch — and get an answer that’s less about the craft of dressing oneself and more about what we owe one another. What do clothes mean to him? Pace explains that his husband, fashion executive Matthew Foley, will often pause and tell people, “Thank you for your elegance.” Pace knows what he means. He begins to quote the English poet John Milton about what different types of garments mean in different settings, but decides to explain it a simpler way. “When you see a beautiful woman dressed …” he trails off. “Thank you! You’ve made my day!”


	And his day was made, time and again, by Kidman and Bullock. “They’re so cool in this movie,” Pace says, sounding more like the nose-pressed-against-glass Texan than the Milton-scholar movie star. “It’s, like, everything you want.” 

	Pace has no particular expectation for where the film will take him, although — whether or not “Practical Magic 2” can harness the same nostalgic stardust that “The Devil Wears Prada 2” did earlier this year — it may open up new career possibilities. But Pace doesn’t have any next role in mind. What matters is a scene partner with whom he can build a relationship. “Who will be the man that I play, or woman, or alien? Right now, it’s a blank slate.”

	Which suits him just fine. “When you’re trying to entertain the masses, people can put labels on a job that doesn’t need labels,” says friend and former co-star Powell. “What’s really brilliant about Lee is that he fights that at every turn. He’s truly chasing interest — his own interest.” Powell notes just how often Pace obscures himself (including, in “Practical Magic 2,” his shroud of fake tattoos): “For being the most handsome man in Hollywood, he sure loves masks.” 

	But Pace needed to hide less, perhaps, for “Practical Magic 2.” The romantic tones represented a chance to think about love, not war. On-screen, he’s often been powerful and threatening, but in life, he’s thinking about matters of the heart. This private actor, explaining it, lets me in a little. “I don’t think about love in the abstract,” he says. “I think about the people. Love is a feeling, a chemistry with someone — an agreement. Let’s be a little more open with each other. I trust you. Let’s trust.” He laughs. “Still — it’s just the greatest riddle, isn’t it?”

title: ‘The Trial of Alec Baldwin’ Trailer: Actor Gives Documentary Crew Full Access to His Life in the Aftermath of Deadly ‘Rust’ Shooting
description: A trailer has been released for Oscar-nominated director Rory Kennedy’s long-awaited documentary, “The Trial of Alec Baldwin.” The film, which follo
body:
A trailer has been released for Oscar-nominated director Rory Kennedy’s long-awaited documentary, “The Trial of Alec Baldwin.” The film, which follows the actor after the accidental on-set shooting of cinematographer Halyna Hutchins in 2021, is set to be released in theaters across North America starting Oct. 16. 

	“On October 21, 2021, cinematographer Halyna Hutchins is killed on a movie set by a prop gun held by the actor Alec Baldwin. In the immediate aftermath of the tragedy, virtually no one doubts that it was an accident and a deeply traumatizing experience for everyone involved,” reads the film’s official logline. “After the shock subsides, questions of responsibility, guilt, blame, punishment and justice begin circulating in the media, fueled largely by Baldwin’s fame, as well as his reputation. Talented and adored, yet also flawed, politically outspoken, and prone to explosions of anger, the NYC-based Hollywood star becomes a lightning rod for online haters and a target for pushy paparazzi. With prosecutors weighing criminal charges, the events that unfold are driven less by the facts surrounding the case and more by who Alec Baldwin is — both as a man and as a public figure.” 
	

	Kennedy, who reached out to Baldwin about the project following the news, first began filming the actor in 2023. While initially hesitant, Baldwin agreed and provided the director with full access to his life throughout the process of the trial. (As previously reported by Variety, filming of the documentary began before Baldwin learned that Santa Fe County prosecutors dropped two counts of involuntary manslaughter against him and continued as he stood trial in July 2024.) 
	

	“This story is a tricky one because there is Halyna, who is the victim in this story and I, of course have enormous empathy for Halyna and her family given my own background and experience,” Kennedy told Variety ahead of the documentary’s premiere at the 2025 DOC NYC film festival. “But I think there should be room to see how there can be more than one victim. There can be a spectrum of victims in different situations, and it’s important to have space for that.”

	“The Trial of Alec Baldwin” was produced by Kennedy, Mark Bailey and Julia Marchesi and executive produced by Jared Underwood, Andrew C. Robinson, Colin Marshall, Todd Thompson, Rita Powers, Tanner Cusumano, Rob Guillermo, Ray Maiello, Louis Krubich, Dan Fried, Randy Jones Toll and Steven Toll. 

	Watch the trailer for “The Trial of Alec Baldwin” below.

title: Virginie Efira to Receive Mill Valley Film Festival’s Screen Artistry Award for ‘All of a Sudden’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Virginie Efira will receive the Mill Valley Film Festival (MVFF) Award for Screen Artistry at the festival’s 49th edition, organizers announced. The
body:
Virginie Efira will receive the Mill Valley Film Festival (MVFF) Award for Screen Artistry at the festival’s 49th edition, organizers announced. The actor is honored for her performance in “All of a Sudden,” which screens at the festival.

	Efira shared the Cannes Film Festival award for best actress earlier this year with co-star Okamoto Tao for the same film. “All of a Sudden” marks the French-language debut of director Hamaguchi Ryusuke (“Drive My Car”). In the film, Efira plays Marie-Lou, who runs a care facility outside Paris and pushes for gentler treatment of its elderly residents. A chance encounter with a Japanese playwright, played by Okamoto, sets off a friendship that grows into a reflection on mortality, human connection and mutual obligation.
	

	“Virginie Efira gives a performance of extraordinary grace and quiet power in ‘All of a Sudden,’ grounding its expansive ideas about career, capitalism and politics in our shared humanity and expressing the profound mystery of human connection. We are honored to recognize her with an MVFF Award,” said Rose Kuo, MVFF’s artistic director.


	Mark Fishkin, founder and director of the festival, called “All of a Sudden” a deeply life-affirming film that reminds audiences human beings need each other not just to thrive, but simply to exist. “That’s a message worth sharing with our audience, and Virginie Efira brings it to life with extraordinary heart,” he said.

	Efira has also won a César Award, for Alice Winocour’s “Paris Memories,” and has starred in Paul Verhoeven’s “Elle” and “Benedetta,” as well as Justine Triet’s “In Bed with Victoria” and “Sibyl.”
	

	MVFF49 takes place Oct. 1-11 across venues in Marin County and the Bay Area. The festival is presented by the California Film Institute, a nonprofit that also runs the DocLands Documentary Film Festival. Efira’s honor comes through MVFF’s Spotlight program, which recognizes standout work by film artists at any stage of their careers.

schema.headline: Virginie Efira to Receive Mill Valley Film Festival’s Screen Artistry Award for ‘All of a Sudden’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Emmys 2026 Party Guide With Katherine LaNasa, Quinta Brunson and Richard Gadd
description:
Television’s biggest night of the year is almost here.

	In other words, let the partying begin. The festivities kick off with Gold House’s One Hous
body:
Television’s biggest night of the year is almost here.

	In other words, let the partying begin. The festivities kick off with Gold House’s One House Toast to the Emmys as well as the Creative Coalition’s Humanitarian Awards dinner.

	Agencies like UTA and WME will have pre-parties. So will A24, BAFTA North America, Warner Bros. Television Group and NBCUniversal.


	Champagne will continue to flow after the Emmys ceremony on Monday, with the Television Academy’s Governors Gala and soirees hosted by Netflix, HBO Max, Disney and more.

title: ‘Avatar: Seven Havens’ to Release Three Episodes Per Week as ‘Last Airbender’ Sequel Series Drops New Trailer
description:
“Avatar: Seven Havens” will drop its first season in batches of three episodes per week. 

	As previously announced, the new entry in the “Avatar: T
body:
“Avatar: Seven Havens” will drop its first season in batches of three episodes per week. 

	As previously announced, the new entry in the “Avatar: The Last Airbender” universe will debut on Oct. 9 on Paramount+. Now, Paramount has confirmed that the first three episodes of the first season (or Book 1 in “Avatar” parlance) will premiere on that date, followed by three more episodes each Friday through Oct. 30. Paramount has already greenlit a 13-episode Book 2, the exact premiere date of which will be announced at a later date. 
	

	There is also a new trailer for the highly-anticipated series, which can be seen below. 


	The logline for “Seven Havens” states: 

	“Set in a world shattered by a devastating cataclysm, ‘Avatar: Seven Havens’ follows Pavi, a young Earthbender who discovers she’s the new Avatar after Korra, only to find that in this dangerous era, that title marks her as humanity’s destroyer, not its savior. Hunted by both human and spirit enemies, Pavi and her long-lost twin Nisha must uncover their mysterious origins and save the Seven Havens before civilization’s last strongholds collapse.”

	The voice cast includes Saheli Khan as Pavi, Aishu Devan as Nisha, Akshay Khanna as Karthik, Major Curda as Jae, Sakina Jaffrey as Agam, Darren Barnet as Daemin, Dianne Doan as Zi, and Dee Bradley Baker as Geet and Ruhi.

	“Avatar: Seven Havens” is created by franchise masterminds Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko, who also serve as executive producers via Avatar Studios. Ethan Spaulding is an executive producer as well, with Sehaj Sethi as co-executive producer. Nickelodeon and Avatar Studios produce.
	

	The Oct. 9 premiere date was originally earmarked for the film “Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender,” before that release was moved up to July 25 after the movie leaked online earlier this year. It debuted on Paramount+ directly following a special screening at San Diego Comic-Con. 

	In an interview with Variety around the release of the film, Konietzko spoke about the South Asian influences of “Seven Havens.” 

	“The concept and even the word ‘avatar’ all come from Indian culture and tradition and Sanskrit,” he said. “So we had done a bit in ‘Avatar,’ the original series. We’re obviously inspired by and draw from a lot of real world cultures for our fantasy world. But that said, I kind of felt like with the first two series, we had underserved that inspiration, and so it was very deliberate with Seven Havens to to code Pavi as a South Asian-inspired character.”

schema.headline: ‘Avatar: Seven Havens’ to Release Three Episodes Per Week as ‘Last Airbender’ Sequel Series Drops New Trailer

title: Jennifer Lawrence Speaks Out on Joining Instagram and Warns Toxic Fans: ‘If Anyone Says Anything Negative I Will Quit Immediately’
description: Jennifer Lawrence has officially joined Instagram, earning nearly 1 million followers in less than 24 hours. But the Oscar winner is issuing a warni
body:
Jennifer Lawrence has officially joined Instagram, earning nearly 1 million followers in less than 24 hours. But the Oscar winner is issuing a warning to toxic social media users: She will quit Instagram if people start being mean.

	“So yeah, I am giving it a shot and if anyone says anything negative I will quit immediately, no questions asked,” Lawrence said in her first video post on her Instagram feed. “If anyone thinks something mean, I will know and I will quit.”
	

	Lawrence doubled down on her message in a post on her Instagram story that reads: “Please be mindful that any mean or aggressive comments can negatively affect the baby. It’s me. I’m the baby.”


	When launching her Instagram account on Sept. 9, Lawrence told fans that she was using the @jlaw handle because @jenniferlawrence was already taken. She posted her first video the following day. As of the posting of this article, Lawrence is following 46 accounts that vary from Miss Piggy (she is currently developing a Miss Piggy movie with friend and fellow Oscar winner Emma Stone) to Martin Scorsese and Leonardo DiCaprio, with whom she recently shot the psychological drama “What Happens at Night” (the movie is expected to release next year from Apple). 

	Some of Lawrence’s other follows include her “Hunger Games” co-star Josh Hutcherson, Ziwe, Stephen Colbert, Suki Waterhouse, “Chicken Shop Date” host Amelia Dimoldenberg, Daniel Kaluuya, Evan Ross Katz, Kim Kardashian, Khloe Kardashian, Kourtney Kardashian, Kylie Jenner, Kendall Jenner, Kris Jenner, Matt Rogers, Bowen Yang, Keke Palmer, Derek Blasberg, NPR, Jonathan Anderson, Andy Cohen, Emily Ratajkowski, Amy Poehler, Ms. Rachel, Amy Schumer, Alex Consani,  Dakota Johnson, her husband Cooke Maroney and more.
	

	Despite leading one of the biggest Hollywood franchises of the 21st century with “The Hunger Games” and earning various award wins and nominations, Lawrence has stayed off social media until now. She’s been vocal in past interviews about disliking press tours because she “loses control” of her craft as interviews and headlines go viral. Perhaps joining social media will allow Lawrence to get some of that control back.

	Watch Lawrence’s first Instagram post in the video below.

title: Amalie Næsby Fick on Toronto-Bound ‘What Lies Between Us’ and Challenging Viewers: Would You Defend Your Child, No Matter What? (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Variety has been given exclusive access “What Lies Between Us” (“Dobbeltfejl”), selected for Toronto’s Discovery section and one of three short-list
body:
Variety has been given exclusive access “What Lies Between Us” (“Dobbeltfejl”), selected for Toronto’s Discovery section and one of three short-listed Danish pics to become Denmark’s Oscar entry.The feature (formerly known as “Good Mothers”) reunites some of Denmark’s finest talents on both sides of the camera: the stars of the cult series “Borgen” — Sidse Babette Knudsen and “The Killing”— Sofie Gråbøl, in their first joint screen appearance; Asta Kamma August, currently playing in Hans Petter Moland’s San Sebastian main competition entry “Growth of the Soil;” Zentropa producer Louise Vesth, s long-time collaborator of Lars von Trier; and Nikolaj Arcel (“A Royal Affair,” “The Promised Land”) who co-penned the script with Sara Isabella Jønsson (“Copenhagen Cowboy,” “Unruly”).


	Making her live action feature debut is Amalie Næsby Fick, behind the Berlinale Generation animation pic “The Incredible Story of a Giant Pear,” and the Netflix series “Baby Fever.”
	

	Set in a small community, the story takes a deep dive into the complex world of modern parenthood, asking the uncomfortable question: How far would you go to protect your child in a crisis situation? Would you lie, break the law, betray your friends and family?The storyline turns on a scandal that shakes a small Danish suburban town when a teen boy accuses two of his peers of sexual assault. When Anne Sofie (Sidse Babette Knudsen) the successful real estate agent and tennis fanatic discovers that her son Frederik (Viktor Garrison) might be more involved than she thought, her moral compass wavers and she takes a drastic decision to save her family and reputation. At the same time, her long-time friendship with Sarah (Sofie Gråbøl) mother of Oskar (August Mejlva-Aaen) takes a hit, while Ulrikke (Asta August), the third embroiled mother tries to navigate the crisis as wel as being single mum of the troubled NC (Julian Brix).In the clip shared by Zentropa and sales rep TrustNordisk, Anne Sofie’s family tries to get on with life as usual, while a police car is patrolling in front of their home.



	When producer Louise Vesth first approached Fick with a possible adaptation of the yet-to-be published book “Dobbelfejl” by author Anne Mette Kirk in 2023, she jumped on the offer. As a mother of a young boy, she immediately related to the core of the story  – would you defend your child-no matter what?

	“I read the book which was a true page-turner, and told Louise I’d love to do a screen adaptation and use the interesting premise as a thriller engine in the film,” Fick tells Variety.
	

	Eager to make the material hers, the helmer had the idea of focusing on Anne Sofie, the mother with the most questionable behaviour, morally and ethically. 

	“I felt Anne Sofie has the most interesting journey,” says Fick who was keen to explore how her determination to protect her son, no matter what, affects her judgment and her own behaviour. “In all my films and series, I’m interested in characters doing the wrong things, yet we still root for them.”

	References for the pic ranged from Ang Lee’s “The Ice Storm,” “for the drama with a thriller engine,” to HBO’s “Big Little Lies, “for the family drama and smalltown community feeling”, although the helmer was adamant not to set the story in an affluent environment. “The crisis situation could happen to anyone, it had to be about ‘normal’ middle class families” Fick says.Reese Witherspoon’s fierce character [Madeline Martha Mckenzie] in “Big Little Lies,” her pulling power in the community and in the school was another inspiration for the character of Anne Sofie, says Fick who knew from a very early stage that she wanted Knudsen for the part, next to Gråbøl as Sarah.

	“Sidse is warm, witty and humorous; She has the ability to portray nuanced characters. She can do the most dreadful things, yet you still root for her. As for Sofie, she is as talented and extremely funny in real life. She has a pulling power and gets you fully engrossed in any character,” says Fick who was also thrilled to bring together the two heavyweight Danish actors for the first time. “Both played earlier in Susanne Bier’s comedy “The One and Only” [1999], but they had no scenes together. This is their very first time!” Fick beams.

	Sidse Babette Knudsen On Her Role

	Discussing her character with Variety, Knudsen says about Anne Sofie: “She´s a fighter. She used to be a tennis champion in her youth, and it has created a need in her to be a winner. She regards conflicts as fights, where she intimidates and overpowers the opposing part. Her life is great until it isn’t, and she believes that she is fighting for her son.”

	“When she finds herself out of bounds, having forced and manipulated and lied, there is no way back for her than to take her cover story all the way.

	“Tennis is an important arena in the film,” adds Knudsen. “Her relationship with her son is seen on the tennis court, how she helps, loves, coaches, punishes and ultimately sees her son.”
	

	A novice in kids casting, Fick said she relied on the seasoned Anja Philip (“Borgen,” “Margrete-Queen of the North”) who helped her cast the young Garrison, Mejlva-Aaen and Brix, selected picked among 200 boys.

	“We were extremely careful in our approach to the sensitive subject [of sexual assault] with the young actors, letting them know the full story and our intention,” Fick underscores. “We had lots of rehearsals, helping them map out their character, then Anja who’s worked on almost everything I’ve made, was on set for the most difficult scenes.”On her first experience of directing a live feature, Fick said having “a trustful and creative collaboration” with Vesth, Arcel, Jønsson and the entire crew was quintessential. “I felt safe and in very good hands.”So how would she – as a parent –  react if her kid was suddenly accused of a crime or misdemeanour? “I would probably go all the way – lie, cheat, do anything to protect my child!” says Fick with a grin.Ultimately, she hopes that audiences will be engaged in the story, reflect and openly discuss challenging topics such as sexual assault, bullying at school, and the difficulty of parenting.

	The film will hit Danish theaters Sept. 24 via Nordisk Film Distribution.

schema.headline: Amalie Næsby Fick on Toronto-Bound ‘What Lies Between Us’ and Challenging Viewers: Would You Defend Your Child, No Matter What? (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Philippines Ferry Inferno: Five Dead, Nearly 100 Missing as Fiery Video is Released
description:

                          Five Dead, Nearly 100 Missing ...
body:
Philippines Ferry Inferno
                          Five Dead, Nearly 100 Missing ...
                          Watch The Insane Video
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 10, 2026
                            5:57 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 10, 2026
                                7:22 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            A ferry in the Philippines went up in flames Wednesday, killing at least 5 people ... with almost 100 others missing as authorities released horrifying video of the tragic incident.
      
    
            The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) released the footage on Facebook, showing the MV June Aster as a floating inferno with 117 passengers and 17 crew members onboard the boat, which was reportedly traveling near the tourist town of Coron in Palawan province. The five people who were deceased were taken to an emergency evacuation and rescue center in Coron.
      
    
      
      At least five people have been killed and over 80 are unaccounted for after a fire broke out on a ferry in the Philippines.Footage shows the MV June Aster ablaze in waters near the tourist hotspot of Coron in the Palawan district.Search and rescue efforts are ongoing. pic.twitter.com/6f7YUMyT51
              @JMChyno
  
    
            A PCG spokesperson said they launched a search party for those who were unaccounted for and have reportedly rescued 43 people so far. One survivor told officials they heard an explosion emanating from a compartment on the boat that holds a number of vehicles and motorbikes. 
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The spokesperson also said first responders are still fighting the fire, but have yet to put out the flames. The cause of the blaze is still under investigation.
      
    
            The owner of the MV June Aster issued a statement ... saying the company was profoundly sad and deeply concerned about the massive fire raging on the boat.

                            6:57 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Barry Melrose, the former NHL player, coach and longtime ESPN hockey analyst, has died ... his wife, Cindy, told ESPN.
      
    
            Melrose joined ESPN in 1996 and retired in 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He was best known for coaching Wayne Gretzky and the Los Angeles Kings to the 1993 Stanley Cup Final before becoming one of hockey’s most recognizable TV personalities.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            ESPN praised Melrose as a "distinctive and trusted" voice whose passion for the sport was unmistakable.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He was also known for his flashy suits, signature mullet and goatee ... and was beloved by colleagues and fans alike.
      
    
            Barry was 70.
      
    
            RIP.
